lead: A vapour compression refrigerator needs a compressor, and a compressor needs shaft work, normally electricity. A vapour absorption refrigerator replaces it with a liquid that soaks up the refrigerant vapour, a small pump that lifts the liquid to condenser pressure, and a generator that boils the refrigerant out again with heat. That heat can be waste steam, engine exhaust or solar. The machine has almost no moving parts. This chapter traces the two loops, names the fluid pairs, and defines the COP used for absorption machines, which is not the COP of a compressor-driven chiller.
prereq: You need Chapter 6.7 (the vapour compression cycle and its COP) and the steady flow energy balance from Unit 2.

sections.h3: The compressor's job, done by a liquid

blocks.text: In the vapour compression cycle (see 6.7) the compressor does one job: lift vapour from evaporator pressure to condenser pressure. Vapour is bulky, so squeezing it costs real work, and that work must come from a motor.

A liquid is not bulky. Dissolve the refrigerant vapour in a liquid and the mixture can be pumped up to condenser pressure by a small pump that handles a trickle of liquid, not a flood of vapour. The pump work is a small fraction of the compressor work. The price: the refrigerant must now be driven out of the liquid at that high pressure, and that takes heat.

The vessel where the vapour is dissolved is the absorber. The vessel where heat drives it out is the generator. Absorber, pump and generator together do the compressor's job, and the running bill changes from electricity to heat.

The absorbent must have two habits. It must soak up refrigerant vapour eagerly at the absorber's low pressure and low temperature. And it must release the refrigerant readily when warmed in the generator. Ammonia in water, and water in lithium bromide, both qualify.
Six components carry two loops that meet in the absorber and in the generator. First, the refrigerant loop:

items: Generator: heat Q<sub>G</sub> boils refrigerant out of the solution; high-pressure vapour leaves for the condenser.
Condenser: the vapour rejects heat and condenses to liquid at condenser pressure.
Expansion valve: the pressure falls to evaporator level at nearly constant enthalpy.
Evaporator: the liquid boils, taking heat Q<sub>E</sub> from the load. This is the cooling.
Absorber: the low-pressure vapour is taken up by weak solution, and heat Q<sub>A</sub> is rejected to keep the absorber cool.
Pump: strong solution (rich in refrigerant) is pumped from the absorber up to generator pressure. W<sub>p</sub> is small because the fluid is liquid.
Solution heat exchanger: the hot weak solution leaving the generator warms the cold strong solution going in, saving generator heat.
Generator: the heat drives the refrigerant off; the solution becomes weak and returns to the absorber through a throttle.

blocks.text: Only the compression end is new. The condenser, expansion valve and evaporator are the ones from 6.7, and the two pressures are still set by the condenser and evaporator temperatures. The solution heat exchanger is optional in principle and fitted in practice; it moves heat inside the machine, so it changes no energy balance on the whole unit.

Ammonia-water. Ammonia is the refrigerant (it boils at about −33 °C at one atmosphere) and water is the absorbent. It reaches sub-zero evaporator temperatures, so it serves cold stores and food freezing. Water is volatile, so some water vapour leaves the generator with the ammonia and must be knocked out in a rectifier before the condenser.

Lithium bromide-water. Water is the refrigerant and lithium bromide, a non-volatile salt, is the absorbent. There is nothing to rectify. But water freezes at 0 °C, so the machine chills water to about 5 to 7 °C for air conditioning and cannot do freezing duty. Too strong or too cold a solution crystallises and blocks the pipes.
The output of the machine is the cooling Q<sub>E</sub> at the evaporator. The input we pay for is the generator heat Q<sub>G</sub>, plus a small pump work W<sub>p</sub>.

blocks.where: Q<sub>E</sub> is the heat taken in at the evaporator, that is, the cooling, in kW; Q<sub>G</sub> is the heat supplied to the generator, in kW; W<sub>p</sub> is the pump work, in kW. All three are rates, so the ratio is dimensionless.

blocks.text: The denominator is not the same as in vapour compression, where only compressor work is counted. Never mix the two: a COP of 0.65 and a COP of 4 are numbers about different purchases.

A single-effect lithium bromide-water machine reaches about 0.5 to 0.7. A vapour compression chiller of the same duty reaches 3 to 5. By that measure absorption is five to eight times worse, and it often does not matter, because the generator heat is waste: steam you were going to dump, exhaust from a genset, or solar heat from a collector with no fuel bill. Heat is cheap where electricity is not, and the machine has one small pump instead of a compressor, so wear and starting current are low.
A COP below 1 breaks no law. Energy in equals energy out: the condenser and absorber together reject Q<sub>E</sub> + Q<sub>G</sub> + W<sub>p</sub>, always more than the cooling delivered.

examples.question: A vapour absorption chiller produces 100 kW of cooling from 150 kW of heat supplied to its generator. The solution pump consumes 2 kW. Find (a) the COP of the machine and (b) the total heat rejected in the condenser and the absorber together.
steps: Data: Q<sub>E</sub> = 100 kW, Q<sub>G</sub> = 150 kW, W<sub>p</sub> = 2 kW.
Steady flow energy balance on the whole machine: energy in = energy out. Energy in = Q<sub>E</sub> + Q<sub>G</sub> + W<sub>p</sub> = 100 + 150 + 2 = 252 kW.
Energy out = Q<sub>condenser</sub> + Q<sub>absorber</sub>, since no other stream leaves.
examples.answer: COP = 0.658, and the condenser and absorber together reject 252 kW.

traps: Dividing by pump work alone, or copying the vapour compression COP. The absorption COP divides the cooling by Q<sub>G</sub> + W<sub>p</sub>; the generator heat is the main input.
Using a Carnot expression such as T<sub>E</sub>/(T<sub>G</sub> − T<sub>E</sub>). That is a reversible-work limit; absorption machines are rated on measured heat input.
Naming lithium bromide as the refrigerant. In the LiBr-water pair water is the refrigerant and the salt is the absorbent; in ammonia-water the ammonia is the refrigerant.
Forgetting the pump work in the overall balance. Adding only Q<sub>E</sub> and Q<sub>G</sub> leaves the rejected heat short by W<sub>p</sub>.
Reversing the two vessels: the generator receives heat, the absorber rejects heat.

quiz.q: Which component of a vapour compression cycle is absent in a vapour absorption cycle, and which components take over its function?
quiz.a: The compressor is absent. The absorber, the solution pump and the generator together raise the refrigerant from evaporator pressure to condenser pressure.

quiz.q: In the lithium bromide-water pair, name the refrigerant and the absorbent.
quiz.a: Water is the refrigerant; lithium bromide is the absorbent.

quiz.q: Why is the pump work in an absorption machine so much smaller than the compressor work for the same duty?
quiz.a: The pump handles liquid, which is dense, while the compressor handles low-pressure vapour of very large specific volume. For the same mass flow the volume to be displaced, and hence the work, is far smaller.

quiz.q: Why does the absorption COP use Q<sub>G</sub> in the denominator rather than W<sub>p</sub> alone?
quiz.a: The generator heat is the main paid input; the pump work is a small extra. The COP must compare the cooling with everything supplied, so both appear, with Q<sub>G</sub> dominating.

quiz.q: An absorption chiller gives 175 kW of cooling while its generator takes 260 kW of heat; the pump uses 3 kW. Find the COP and the total heat rejected by the condenser and absorber.
An absorption chiller with COP 0.65 rejects far more heat at the condenser and absorber than it removes at the evaporator. Explain why this must be so, using an energy balance.
quiz.a: The unit receives Q<sub>E</sub> at the evaporator, Q<sub>G</sub> at the generator and W<sub>p</sub> at the pump, and delivers no work. Steady state therefore requires Q<sub>condenser</sub> + Q<sub>absorber</sub> = Q<sub>E</sub> + Q<sub>G</sub> + W<sub>p</sub>, which is larger than Q<sub>E</sub>. A COP below 1 means Q<sub>G</sub> alone already exceeds Q<sub>E</sub>, so most of the rejected heat is generator heat passed through the machine.

quiz.q: Why can a lithium bromide-water chiller not be used to freeze food at −10 °C, while an ammonia-water machine can?
quiz.a: In LiBr-water the refrigerant is water, which freezes at 0 °C, so the evaporator cannot run below that and the chilled fluid stays near 5 to 7 °C. In ammonia-water the refrigerant is ammonia, which boils at about −33 °C at one atmosphere, so evaporator temperatures well below zero are possible.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial machines stack a second generator on the same principle, using higher-pressure steam, to reach roughly double the single-effect COP. Diffusion-absorption refrigerators with no pump at all, driven by a gas flame, use the same absorber-generator pair. Solar cooling couples a flat-plate or evacuated-tube collector to a single-effect lithium bromide-water chiller. Search 'double-effect absorption chiller', 'GAX cycle' and 'solar cooling' to go further; the concentration charts and crystallisation limits are covered in the refrigeration elective.
